You lost that argument last winter.

I say to the Hon. Member that this argument is far from lost. We are only now beginning to see the kind of economic impact that this Free Trade Agreement will bring to the people. This argument is far from over.
The election is over.

This is only one example of the kind of economic impact that the rationalization of industry can hold when it has gone head to head with American counterparts in light of the tariff reductions through trade. Many Members on the other side of the House and many members of the business community have said this is the reality of life. To some extent, perhaps they are right. However, I want to remind the House that the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) made a commitment during the election that any jobs lost through the trade agreement would be recovered through a massive restructuring program and job creation program that would be assured by the Government if the Free Trade Agreement saw the light of day.
We are in the middle of free trade now, but I do not see any evidence of that massive job creation program that was promised by the Government.
I want to turn to another area of concern, an industry that I think will be hit probably the hardest as a result of the effects of free trade. It is the tourism industry.
Apart from the lip service which the Government gave earlier in terms of providing tourism with the kind of profile that is needed to recognize it as the growth industry of the future, the Government has continued to keep the tourism ministry buried within the bowels of the larger ministry, that being the Department of Industry, Science and Technology. What a strange place for tourism to be hidden. If an industry is going to be given the profile it needs, it must be given a full fledged ministry. The Tourism Industry Association of Canada has been calling for that for some time. The Government has not kept its commitment. The removal of the Regional Economic Development Programs, of which
tourism programs are a part, will make it increasingly difficult for this industry to develop the kind of marketing and product development that is needed in our regions across the country.
I realize that my time is up. I will simply conclude by saying that there is much at fault with the current Budget. I believe that the economic impact of the Budget will be felt for some time, particularly throughout the further regions of this country.

Madam Speaker, I would be happy to see the clock if other Members want, but I will profitably use the three minutes remaining. In addressing the economic programs of the Government in such a short time, it is hard to decide on which of the many things one wants to talk about.
In the three minutes that I have, I would like to speak about the proposal to close military bases in depressed and developing regions of our country which would benefit tremendously from having these continue, as they are a very important part of those communities.
When I heard the announcement, it reminded me of a tactic I learned about in the United States known as the Washington Monument ploy. I learned about this from a cabinet colleague in the United States who said that when the Department of the Interior ever faced the prospect of a budget cut, it would put up a sign announcing that the Washington Monument would be closed because of cut-backs in its budget. This monument is visited by 3,000 people an hour and, within a couple of hours, the Department of the Interior would have the crowd lobbying on Capital Hill to keep the expenditures of the Department of the Interior intact.
I had a similar experience once as Solicitor General, when the Mounties were asked to cut their budget. They came back telling me that the first thing to be cut would be the Musical Ride.
When I saw that the base at Summerside would be closed, I thought instantly of the Washington Monument ploy. When one goes to the heart of it, it is an attempt by bureaucrats to get the public on their side in a battle against politicians. For the purposes of this argument, I am not saying that the Government should not always look for cuts that it can make in the Budget, but when
